title: Ananse and the Pot of Wisdom

pages.text: Long ago, when the world was new, Kwaku Ananse the spider had an idea. “People are always coming to me for advice,” he said. “Imagine if I owned all the wisdom in the world. Then everyone would have to come to me, and they would have to pay.” So Ananse took a large clay pot and set off. He went from village to village, from forest to river. Wherever he found a piece of wisdom, he dropped it into the pot. At last the pot was full, and Ananse was sure that there was no wisdom left anywhere but there.
sentences: Long ago, when the world was new, Kwaku Ananse the spider had an idea.
“People are always coming to me for advice,” he said.
“Imagine if I owned all the wisdom in the world.
Then everyone would have to come to me, and they would have to pay.” So Ananse took a large clay pot and set off.
He went from village to village, from forest to river.
Wherever he found a piece of wisdom, he dropped it into the pot.
At last the pot was full, and Ananse was sure that there was no wisdom left anywhere but there.
pages.alt: A thin spider in a strip of kente carrying a large clay pot along a forest path past a village.

pages.text: Ananse carried the pot home and shut the door. He did not tell his wife, Aso, what was in it. He did not tell his son, Ntikuma. But a new worry kept him awake. “What if somebody steals it?” he thought. “I must hide it where nobody can reach.” Behind the village stood a silk-cotton tree, the tallest tree in the forest, with a trunk as straight as a spear. “I will tie the pot to the very top,” said Ananse. “Then all the wisdom in the world will be mine alone, for ever.”

He did not tell his wife, Aso, what was in it.
He did not tell his son, Ntikuma.
But a new worry kept him awake.
“What if somebody steals it?” he thought.
“I must hide it where nobody can reach.” Behind the village stood a silk-cotton tree, the tallest tree in the forest, with a trunk as straight as a spear.
“I will tie the pot to the very top,” said Ananse.
“Then all the wisdom in the world will be mine alone, for ever.”
pages.alt: A spider lying awake beside a clay pot inside a hut, with a very tall straight tree visible through the window.

pages.text: Before sunrise, Ananse crept out with the pot. He tied it round his neck with a rope so that it hung in front of his belly. Then he began to climb. But the pot was in the way. It bumped against the trunk and pushed him off. His eight legs could not reach round it. He climbed a little and slid down. He climbed again and slid down again. The sun rose higher. Ananse was sweating and muttering, and he had not climbed the height of a man. A bird in the branches laughed at him.

Then he began to climb.

His eight legs could not reach round it.
He climbed a little and slid down.
He climbed again and slid down again.
The sun rose higher.
Ananse was sweating and muttering, and he had not climbed the height of a man.
A bird in the branches laughed at him.
pages.alt: A spider struggling to climb a huge tree trunk with a clay pot hanging in front of his belly.

pages.text: Ananse did not know that he was being watched. Little Ntikuma had woken, missed his father, and followed him. For a long time the boy stood quietly at the foot of the tree. At last he could keep silent no longer. “Father,” he called, “why do you carry the pot in front of you? Tie it on your back. Then your legs will be free to hold the tree.” Ananse looked down. He was annoyed. But he was also tired, so he moved the pot round to his back. Up he went, as easily as walking.

Little Ntikuma had woken, missed his father, and followed him.
For a long time the boy stood quietly at the foot of the tree.
At last he could keep silent no longer.
“Father,” he called, “why do you carry the pot in front of you?
Tie it on your back.
Then your legs will be free to hold the tree.” Ananse looked down.
He was annoyed.
But he was also tired, so he moved the pot round to his back.
Up he went, as easily as walking.
pages.alt: A small spider at the foot of a tall tree calling up to a larger spider who is looking down in surprise.

pages.text: Halfway up, Ananse stopped. A thought had struck him like a stone. “I have all the wisdom in the world in this pot,” he said, “and yet my own small son had a piece of wisdom that I did not have. Then the pot is not full after all. And if a child can be wiser than I am, what use is the pot?” He was so angry and ashamed that he tore the pot from his back and flung it down. It struck a root and smashed into a hundred pieces.

And if a child can be wiser than I am, what use is the pot?” He was so angry and ashamed that he tore the pot from his back and flung it down.
It struck a root and smashed into a hundred pieces.
pages.alt: A clay pot shattering on the roots of a great tree while a spider clings to the trunk above.

pages.text: Just then, a great wind blew through the forest. It caught up all the wisdom from the broken pot and carried it over the whole world. A little fell on every village and every house. Men, women, and children each picked up some. Nobody got all of it, and nobody was left with none. That is why, to this day, no one person knows everything, and why even a small child may know what an elder does not. The Akan say that one head does not hold a council. As for Ananse, he went home and listened to his son.

Men, women, and children each picked up some.

That is why, to this day, no one person knows everything, and why even a small child may know what an elder does not.
The Akan say that one head does not hold a council.
As for Ananse, he went home and listened to his son.
pages.alt: A swirling wind carrying small sparkling lights across villages and forests towards the horizon.

activities.question: Why did Ananse want to collect all the wisdom in the world?
options: To share it fairly with everyone
So that everyone would have to come to him and pay
To give it to his son

activities.question: Why could Ananse not climb the tree at first?
options: The pot hung in front of him and got in the way
The tree was covered in thorns

activities.question: Why did Ananse throw the pot down?
options: It was too heavy to carry
He realised his child had wisdom he lacked, so the pot could not hold it all

activities.question: Apply it: In a group project, the group leader refuses to listen to the youngest member’s idea. Using the tale, what would you tell the leader?
options: Good ideas can come from anyone, so listen to everyone

activities.prompt: Put the events of the story in order.
items: Ananse collects wisdom in a clay pot
He decides to hide the pot at the top of the silk-cotton tree
He fails to climb with the pot in front of him
Ntikuma tells him to tie the pot on his back
Ananse throws the pot down and the wind scatters the wisdom
